title: Outdoor Learning Missions
goal: Ten scavenger hunt missions you can take on any walk: a micro-world hunt, a signs-of-life hunt, a water cycle hunt, a geologist's rock hunt and more. Each one has 12 things to find and 3 Extras for going deeper. Your kid searches, ticks off finds and explains why each one counts. Observation, science thinking and clear describing, on a plain old walk.
need: These missions, on your phone or printed
Any outdoor place: a yard, a park, a trail, a beach
Optional: a pencil to tick off finds

lesson.text: A find only counts when your kid can say why it fits. That's the difference between a scavenger hunt and real science: evidence.

model.line: A pinecone chewed right down to the core.
On a stump under a big spruce tree.
A pile of scales all around it, and tooth marks.
A squirrel sat here and ate it, probably this morning.

lesson.modelNote: That's from Mission 2, Signs of life. When your kid says 'found one,' ask: where, what's the clue, and what do you think happened?

academics.subject: Science
academics.text: habitats, animal evidence, water cycle, plants, rocks and soil

academics.subject: Writing
academics.text: precise describing words and short claims backed by clues

academics.subject: Life skills
academics.text: patience, curiosity and caring for a place

howTo.intro: No teaching background needed, and you don't need to know the answers. Read the mission out loud, let your kid lead the search, and ask 'why does that count?' When they're stuck, give a hint, not the answer: 'Where might you find that: near water, in the shade, on a tree?'

plan.what: Pick one mission and a place, and set a boundary.
Search and tick off finds, then try an Extra. About 20 to 45 minutes.
Ask: favourite find? Trickiest one? What should we hunt next time?

troubleshoot.a: That's fine. Circle the missing ones and finish the mission another day, or in another place.
Slow it down with the Claim: each find needs one clue that proves it counts.

skills.name: Observation
skills.text: finding details most people walk past

skills.name: Evidence
skills.text: backing up a find with a clue

skills.name: Stewardship
skills.text: noticing how people affect a place

levelsLine: Every mission has three levels. Explore: find what you can. Develop: find all 12. Extend: do the Extras and explain your best evidence.

themes.title: Micro-world hunt
themes.rule: Become a mini scientist: find the small details most people walk right past.

cards.t: Something smaller than your pinky nail
A tiny hole in soil, wood or a leaf
A tiny hook: a thorn or a burr
A tiny shelter under bark or a stone
A tiny trail: an ant line or a snail path
A miniature forest of moss or grass
Something tiny and bright: a flower, a berry, a beetle

extras: Explore a 1-foot square for 3 minutes and list everything in it.
Draw a micro-map showing where 5 of your finds are.
Describe 3 finds with size words: speck-sized, grainy, pinhead.

themes.title: Signs of life hunt
themes.rule: You're not looking for animals. You're looking for evidence that they were here.

cards.t: Fur or hair caught on something
A chewed cone, nut or seed shell
A burrow or hole that looks used
A resting spot: flattened grass or a worn patch
Scratch marks on dirt or wood
An animal path through the grass
A spider web with repairs or prey
A nest or anything an animal built

extras: For 3 signs, make a claim: 'I think ___ did this because ___.'
Rank your 3 strongest clues and say why they convince you.
Make a case file: evidence, suspect, reason.

themes.title: Texture hunt
themes.rule: Use your sense of touch to compare surfaces and find out how nature protects, soaks up and adapts.
extras: Describe 5 textures with comparisons: like sandpaper, like velvet.
Sort them: armour (protects), sponge (soaks up), blanket (keeps warm).
Pick the best texture for a shelter wall and defend your choice.

themes.title: Colour hunt
themes.rule: Collect nature's colours like a designer: find the shades and hidden colours, not just red and blue.

cards.t: A surprise colour you didn't expect

extras: Line up your finds from lightest to darkest and take a photo.
Make a habitat palette and give it a name, like 'Rainy Trail Neutrals'.
Find 2 camouflage colours. What could each one help hide?

themes.title: Nature engineering hunt
themes.rule: Spot nature's engineering: how things handle wind, water, weight and time.

cards.t: Something that soaks up water: moss or soil
Something shaped to travel: a winged seed, a burr
Something waterproof: a waxy leaf, bark
A natural anchor: roots or a wedged rock

extras: Build a mini bridge, tower or shelter from fallen things, then do a wind test.
Name the force at work in 3 finds: gravity, wind, water or weight.
Pick one nature invention people could copy. How would they use it?

themes.title: Soundscape hunt
themes.rule: Listen like a scientist and find the sounds that make this place feel alive.

cards.t: A mystery sound you can't name
A sound that changes when you move

extras: Draw a sound map: you in the middle, each sound placed where it came from.
Compare two spots, like open field and forest. Which has more kinds of sound?
Try 60 seconds of total silence, then list what you heard.

themes.title: Human impact hunt
themes.rule: Notice how people affect nature, and choose one small thing you can do to help.

cards.t: A sign that protects a place
A healthy spot: clean, lots of growth
A stressed spot: bare or damaged
Something built to help: a bridge, steps, a marked path
A footprint in mud, sand or snow
A piece of litter (pick up only if it's safe)
One helpful thing you can do today

extras: Pick one problem and think of 3 solutions: one a kid can do, one a whole town could do.
Write a one-sentence promise to this place, and why it matters.
Do a tiny cleanup with gloves, if it's safe, and count what you collect.

themes.title: Water cycle hunt
themes.rule: Find how water moves around you: above ground, below ground and in the air.

cards.t: A water source: a stream, a puddle, a lake
Erosion: washed-out soil or bare roots
A plant that loves wet ground
A plant that likes it dry
A drip line under leaves or a roof edge
A filter spot: moss, gravel or roots

extras: Follow a drop: pick a spot and trace where water would go in a big rain.
Find 2 water helpers, like roots or moss, and explain what they do.
Pour a little water on the ground and watch where it flows.

themes.title: Plant detective hunt
themes.rule: Notice plant features like a real naturalist: shape, bark, leaves and survival tricks.

cards.t: A seed container: a cone or a pod
A thorn, a prickle or a burr
A plant growing in a tough spot
A plant with a strong smell
A berry or fruit (look, don't eat)

extras: Pick 3 finds and explain what helps each plant survive: defence, saving water, spreading seeds.
Make a mini key: 4 questions that help identify a tree.
Compare two trees. Which looks older, and what are your clues?

themes.title: Rock and soil hunt
themes.rule: Explore the ground like a geologist, and notice how rocks and soil shape a place.

cards.t: A rock with layers or bands
Soil building up: leaf piles, drifts

extras: Sort your rocks by how they formed: worn by water, broken, or layered.
Squeeze-test the soils with your fingers. Which holds together best, and why might plants care?
Predict which soil grows taller plants, then check what's actually growing.

conclusion.headline: Your kid just turned a walk into fieldwork.
conclusion.text: They searched with a goal, backed up their finds with clues, and noticed things most people walk past every day. Animal evidence, the water cycle, plants, rocks and soil, learned on an ordinary walk.
conclusion.celebrate: Ask about their best evidence: 'Tell me again how you knew a squirrel ate that cone.' Explaining it is what makes it stick.
extensions: Do the same mission in a new season and compare
Do the same mission in a new place: a beach, a city park, a forest
Let your kid write a 12-find mission for you
Keep every finished mission in a folder as a year of fieldwork

signs: They point out tracks, nibbles and nests on ordinary walks
They explain why something counts instead of just pointing
They ask 'which mission today?' before you head out
makeItReal: Take a mission on your next trip. A new place changes every answer: the colours, the sounds, the rocks. Your kid becomes the one teaching you about where you are.
cta: Want the next one? This guide is one of 120+ in the Anywhere Learning library, each with your job and your kid's job at every step.

photo.alt: Two girls poking sticks into water-filled holes in smooth sandstone rock pools
photo.caption: Rock pools: tiny crabs and tadpoles hiding in the holes.

fromHome.text: On a trip to Vancouver Island, we found smooth carved rock full of water-filled holes. My daughter and her friend went from hole to hole, catching tiny crabs and tadpoles. Each hole was its own little world, and that is what these missions are about: slowing down and looking closely at what is right in front of you.
